sections.skill: Calculate costs under a health plan and compare plans using premium, deductible, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum

questions.prompt: Ana's plan has a $1,500 deductible and 20% coinsurance after it, with a $5,000 out-of-pocket maximum. She has spent nothing yet this plan year. A hospital stay has an allowed in-network charge of $10,000 that follows these rules. How much does Ana pay?
questions.intro: Health plans share costs based on the allowed (negotiated) in-network amount. You pay the deductible first. After that, coinsurance means you pay a percent and the plan pays the rest, until you reach the out-of-pocket maximum; then the plan pays 100% of covered in-network costs for the rest of the plan year.
sources: HealthCare.gov (Glossary): Defines premium, deductible, copayment, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum; after the out-of-pocket maximum, the plan pays 100% of covered in-network costs for the rest of the plan year. (https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/)
HealthCare.gov (Young adults): Young adults can generally stay on a parent's health plan until age 26. (https://www.healthcare.gov/young-adults/children-under-26/)
Get Covered New Jersey: New Jersey runs its own health insurance marketplace for individual coverage and financial help. (https://nj.gov/getcoverednj/)
IRS (Working Families Tax Cuts): Beginning in 2026, bronze and catastrophic marketplace plans are treated as HSA-compatible. (https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/working-families-tax-cuts)

questions.prompt: Ana's plan: $1,500 deductible, 20% coinsurance, $5,000 out-of-pocket maximum. In a separate example, with no earlier spending this plan year, a covered in-network stay has an allowed charge of $40,000. How much does Ana pay?
questions.intro: The out-of-pocket maximum caps what you pay for covered in-network care in a plan year (premiums not included).
questions.feedback: $1,500 + 20% × $38,500 = $9,200, but the cap limits her share to $5,000.

misconceptions.C: Takes 20% of the bill and ignores the maximum

In-network care costs the patient less

questions.prompt: In 2026 Ana's health plan has a $500 deductible. It is not an HSA-compatible plan: it is not a qualifying high-deductible plan, a bronze plan, or a catastrophic plan. May she contribute to a health savings account (HSA) for that time?

choices.text: Yes; anyone with any health plan may contribute
Yes, once she turns 65
Yes, if she adds a dental plan
No; her plan is not HSA-compatible

questions.correct_answer: No; her plan is not HSA-compatible
questions.intro: You can contribute to a health savings account (HSA) only while covered by an HSA-compatible plan. Traditionally that meant a qualifying high-deductible health plan; starting in 2026, bronze and catastrophic plans also count. Money in an HSA is pre-tax and carries over year to year.
questions.feedback: Her plan is none of the HSA-compatible types, so she cannot contribute for that time.

misconceptions.B: Invents an age rule; Medicare enrollment actually ends contributions

questions.prompt: An Explanation of Benefits (EOB) says: billed $400; plan discount $150; plan paid $200; patient responsibility $50. What amount does it show Ana is expected to owe the provider?
questions.intro: An EOB is not a bill; it explains what the plan paid and what you may owe. Pay the provider's actual bill after checking that it matches the EOB.
questions.feedback: $400 − $150 − $200 = $50; pay when the provider's bill arrives and matches.
